title: Prepositions after verbs
subtitle: agree with / care for / talk of / ask of
summary: Choose the right preposition after agree, argue, ask, care, know, learn and talk, and notice how the preposition changes the meaning.

lesson.heading: Which prepositions follow these verbs?
lesson.note: The choice is not free: each preposition adds a particular meaning.

lesson.heading: about = concerning a particular thing
lesson.text: **about** is the everyday choice when we mean 'concerning a particular thing'. With **care about** we talk about something we are, or are not, concerned about.

examples.text: They began to learn **about** nutrition when they were at primary school.
He doesn't seem to care **about** the effect a poor diet has on him.

lesson.heading: for = what people want, and looking after
lesson.text: **ask for** is used for what people want, and **argue for** for giving reasons why something is true or right. **care for** means doing the necessary things to keep someone or something in good condition.

examples.text: He finished the drink quickly and asked **for** another.
Many people are arguing **for** a big tax cut.
Jo cared **for** her disabled mother until her death last year.
I don't care **for** the theatre much. / Would you care **for** a cup of coffee?
examples.note: care for = like, or want in an offer - both rather formal

lesson.heading: of = information, and requests
lesson.text: **of** goes with talk, know and learn when we discuss, have or get information. It is a little more formal than about. **ask of** is used when we make or talk about requests.

examples.text: Mira went recently to Laos and can talk **of** nothing else.
The whole country knew **of** Churchill's love of cigars.
I have just learnt **of** the death of Dr Ramirez.
I have a favour to ask **of** you and your sister.

lesson.heading: on and to
lesson.text: **on** goes with talk and agree to mean 'concerned with a particular topic'. Note that **agree to** means that someone allows something to happen.

examples.text: I was asked to talk **on** my research.
We agreed **on** a time to meet.
examples.note: usually there has been previous discussion or disagreement

examples.text: Once the government agreed **to** the scheme it went ahead without delay.

lesson.heading: with = the other person, or the same opinion
lesson.text: **with** follows argue and talk when we go on to mention the person involved. **agree with** says that two people have the same opinion, that we approve of an idea or action, or that two descriptions match.

examples.text: I used to argue / talk **with** Pedro for hours.
Adam thinks we should accept the offer, and I agree **with** him.
I agree **with** letting children choose the clothes they wear.
Stefan's story agreed **with** that of his son.

lesson.text: Ask what the preposition is doing: naming a topic (about, on), a source of information (of), a want (for), or the other person (with).

exercises.prompt: On the website they ask ___ your email address.
We can learn a great deal ___ the oceans by studying even a small piece of coral.
exercises.explanation: learn about = get information concerning a particular thing.

exercises.prompt: I don't care ___ pop music at all. I much prefer classical music.
exercises.explanation: care for = like; it is common in negative sentences and is rather formal.

exercises.prompt: I didn't agree ___ a word of what she said.
exercises.explanation: agree with = have the same opinion as someone, or approve of what is said.

items.text: They began to learn ... nutrition when they were at primary school.
The whole country knew ... Churchill's love of cigars.
He finished the drink quickly and asked ... another.
I have a favour to ask ... you and your sister.
*A:* Dan said he'll try to fix my car. *B:* What does he know ... cars?
Many people are arguing ... a big tax cut.

exercises.prompt: Professor Owen is giving a talk ___ the Romans in Lecture Hall 1.
exercises.explanation: talk on (or about) a topic; talk of is used for having information, not for the subject of a lecture.

exercises.prompt: The teacher says we've got to do the test, so there's no point in arguing ___ it.
exercises.explanation: argue about = disagree concerning a particular thing.

exercises.prompt: She's always arguing ___ her parents about what to watch on television.

exercises.statement: Jo cared about her disabled mother until her death last year.
exercises.explanation: Jo cared for her disabled mother until her death last year. care for = look after; care about = be concerned about.

exercises.prompt: I know it's a lot to ask ___ you, but would you look after the children while I'm in Japan on business?
exercises.explanation: ask of is used when we make or talk about a request.

exercises.prompt: If you know ___ any reasons why you should not be given medical insurance, you must declare them here.
exercises.explanation: know of = have information about; about is unlikely in such a formal context.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the meaning of its verb + preposition.

pairs.left: The police acted on the information very quickly.
pairs.right: did what someone else had advised or suggested

pairs.left: I couldn't be at the meeting, so my solicitor acted for me.
Doctors have called on the Health Minister to resign.
pairs.right: have formally asked her to do it

pairs.left: Campaigners have called for a referendum on the issue.
We're counting on Julia to supply the food for the party.
Playing exciting basketball counts for little if the team isn't winning.
